Testimonial injustice is an ingenuous misjudgement through prejudice, and never a deliberate manipulation of credibility. Hermeneutical injustice is caused by hermeneutical marginalisation and persists despite individual good faith. Both are "discriminatory" epistemic injustice, distinct from distributive kinds. Testimonial injustice can be structural and pre-emptive, as with an un-refreshed list of expert witnesses. | Read |
| [NOTE-859](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-859.md) | Fricker — Powerlessness and Social Interpretation | Hermeneutical injustice is having a significant area of one's social experience obscured from collective understanding owing to hermeneutical marginalisation. It is systematic when the marginalisation is persistent and wide-ranging, and incidental when it is one-off and local, which can happen to a socially powerful subject. A gap with no marginalisation behind it is bad luck. The primary harm is situated hermeneutical inequality. Secondary harms include lost epistemic confidence and the social construction of identity. | Read |
| [NOTE-860](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-860.md) | Fricker — Epistemic Injustice and a Role for Virtue in the Politics of Knowing | A hearer takes testimony critically but without inference, through a socially trained testimonial sensibility. Because that sensibility runs on stereotypes of credibility, it can carry prejudice, and then a speaker receives the wrong degree of credibility through the hearer's unintended prejudice: testimonial injustice. The corrective virtue, reflexive critical openness, is available only where the critical concepts of the time allow it. | Read |
| [NOTE-866](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-866.md) | Hansson — Logic of Belief Revision (SEP, revision of 29 July 2026) | The entry separates two ways of representing what an agent believes: a logically closed belief set, and a belief base whose elements are the beliefs "held independently of any other belief", with everything else "merely derived". Two bases with the same closure can respond differently to the same input (its Abe and Bob example), so the closure is not a sufficient state for revision; belief-set models recover the difference only by attaching a different selection mechanism to the same set. Bases avoid the Recovery postulate, keep distinct inconsistent states apart, and permit operations (external revision, semi-revision by consolidation) that collapse on closed sets. The entry does not discuss keeping reasons, sources or justification records: its only mention of truth maintenance systems is historical, and a base records which beliefs are basic, not why they are held. Iterated revision is treated as an open area in which most proposals carry an ordering of worlds or an entrenchment relation as the state, not a base. | Read |
| [NOTE-874](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-874.md) | Alchourrón, Gärdenfors & Makinson — On the logic of theory change: partial meet contraction and revision | For a logically closed theory A, the contractions satisfying Gärdenfors's six basic postulates are exactly the partial meet contractions, A ∸ x = ⋂γ(A ⊥ x), where γ picks a nonempty subset of the maximal subsets of A not implying x (Observation 2.5); adding the two supplementary postulates gives exactly the contractions whose γ is generated by a transitive relation over those subsets (Corollary 4.5). Revision is defined from contraction by the Levi identity and inherits the corresponding postulates. The result needs, besides A, a selection function or ordering that A itself does not supply: different selection functions give different contractions of the same theory, and in the finite case distinct selection functions always give distinct contractions (Observation 4.6). The setting is one-step change of a single fixed theory; nothing is said about iterated change, about where the selection function comes from, or about the reasons for which a belief is held. | Read |
| [NOTE-955](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-955.md) | Fuchs, Mermin & Schack — an introduction to QBism | QBism in eight pages. Quantum states and all probabilities, 0 and 1 included, are an agent's personal judgements; a measurement is "any action an agent takes to elicit a set of possible experiences", and its outcome is the experience it elicits. The agent applies quantum mechanics to everything external to her, other agents and their reports included, and to nothing but her "own direct internal awareness of her own private experience". Locality follows because one agent's experiences are time-like separated; the Bell parameter λ is set outside physical science. No theorem or model: an interpretive essay. | Read |
| [NOTE-996](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-996.md) | Nichols & Bruno — Intuitions about personal identity | Survey studies of Arizona undergraduates on Williams's personal-identity cases. A transplant case makes memory look necessary for being "still Jim"; a stripped-down Pain case has about 70% say "you will feel the pain" after distinctive mental states are wiped; neither depends on first- or third-person telling, so Williams's explanation by person fails here. Abstract questions and a forced choice favour psychology (over 80%; 64%, p = 0.053). The authors weigh intuitions by robustness and conclude for a psychological criterion conditionally. The results describe a concept under framing; they do not show what persistence is, and the Pain item may test bare sentience, not identity. | Read |
| [NOTE-1035](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1035.md) | Hyzen, Van den Bulck, Puppis, Kulig and Paulussen — Epistemic welfare and algorithmic recommender systems | A theory paper with no data. Epistemic welfare is "creating and maintaining the conditions and capabilities for individuals' epistemic agency in the public sphere". It combines veritistic social epistemology, welfare theory and communication research. Goldman's five standards (reliability, power, fecundity, speed, efficiency) are applied to news media's recommender systems. The paper argues that transparency duties alone, as in the EU AI Act, are not enough, and that profit-optimized recommenders cannot secure epistemic welfare. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1038](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1038.md) | Weatherall, O'Connor and Bruner — How to beat science and influence people | In Bala–Goyal network models with Bayesian policy makers who do not gather evidence, a propagandist who forwards only the real results of unbiased scientists that happen to favour the worse action, or who runs honest studies and publishes only the unfavourable ones, can leave policy makers near-certain of the false theory while the scientists converge on the true one. It works best when the problem is hard, studies are small, scientists are many and policy makers hear few of them. A journalist who reports one result for each side every round slows policy makers' learning and never helps it. | Read |
| [NOTE-1042](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1042.md) | Collins — Learning from the outsider within | Black women intellectuals in sociology are outsiders within: trained into its paradigms but rooted in experience those paradigms omit or distort. From that position they see two kinds of anomaly, omission and distortion, which outsiders lack the professional authority to press and insiders are not placed to see, having produced them. The essay argues this from the content of Black feminist thought, with no study of who detects what; it proposes institutionalizing the tension rather than resolving it. | Read |
| [NOTE-1049](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1049.md) | Kay, Kasirzadeh and Mohamed — Epistemic injustice in generative AI | A conceptual taxonomy, illustrated with reported cases, of four ways generative models can take part in epistemic injustice: amplified and manipulative testimonial injustice, hermeneutical ignorance and access injustice. Its sharpest move is to relocate the testimonial wrong: in the algorithmic setting it "requires a credibility excess assigned to the algorithm". It counts deliberate fabrication as testimonial injustice, which Fricker's account sets apart, and stretches hermeneutical injustice to unequal access to information. Nothing in it is measured by the authors. | Read |
| [NOTE-1056](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1056.md) | Gładziejewski — Real patterns, the predictive mind, and the manifest image | A philosophy paper with no data. It traces Dennett's compression criterion for real patterns through minimum description length and Bayesian inference to variational free energy, so that learning a generative model is extracting real patterns from sensory data. It concludes that the manifest image is a structural description of sensory data, veridical even in a matched vat. The self-model compresses self-generated regularities by positing one common cause, so selves are real as patterns and unreal as substances, and which verdict to give is a dispute over criteria, not facts. It says nothing about consciousness or illusion. | Read |
| [NOTE-1090](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1090.md) | Rogers Commission — Report on the Space Shuttle Challenger accident | The presidential commission's account of Challenger. The physical cause was a field-joint seal design "unacceptably sensitive" to temperature and other factors; the contributing cause was a "flawed" launch decision in which Thiokol's engineers' recommendation against launch was reversed by Thiokol management "at the urging of Marshall", and neither that dispute, the July 1985 launch constraint nor its six waivers reached Levels I and II. The joint had a nine-year history of warnings, accepted erosion and loosened criteria, and the safety, reliability and quality-assurance function was understaffed, subordinate to the offices it checked, and absent from the decision. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-1091](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1091.md) | Aevyra — The Ledger of Will | A careful, self-limiting formal note on what a reduced memory must keep so that an agent can still revise: a retained state supports a declared family of future questions, interventions and changes of evaluative law exactly when those targets are constant on its fibres, and under repeated revision exactly when its fibres lie in the coarsest revision-invariant refinement (Moore–Nerode). The rest is design proposal and an unexecuted experimental protocol. Elementary and correct; the authors say plainly that it synthesizes established ideas. | Read |
| [NOTE-1139](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1139.md) | Miller, Resnick and Zeckhauser — Eliciting informative feedback: the peer-prediction method | A mechanism-design paper with proofs and a worked example. A center with no ground truth pays each rater a strictly proper scoring rule applied to the posterior over a reference rater's report implied by her own report. Truth-telling is a strict Nash equilibrium, payments can be scaled to buy effort and balanced among raters, and coarse reports can be elicited for two types. Uninformative equilibria remain, and collusion, risk aversion, unelicited private signals and trust in the center are left as limits. | Read |
